conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. You're in the emergency department. You came in because of confusion and low blood pressure. We’re going to help you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know you can’t speak, but I’ll explain what’s happening. Your potassium level is very high, which can affect your heart. We’ve given you medicine to bring it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EKG showed changes from high potassium. We also started antibiotics because we think you have pneumonia and a possible urinary infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We replaced your Foley catheter and it drained nearly 2 liters. That means it was blocked. This likely caused kidney stress and part of your illness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re being admitted to the ICU for close monitoring. We’ll keep treating the infection and support your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your potassium is better now—down to 5.9. Your mental status is improving. You’re responding to questions with nods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows pneumonia, likely from aspiration. We’ve started two antibiotics—cefepime and linezolid—to cover the bacteria we suspect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also found Proteus mirabilis in your sputum. It’s sensitive to cefepime, so we’ll continue that. Linezolid may be stopped later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving your first dose of IV antibiotics on the floor. You’ve been moved from ICU because you’re more stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine was high at 2.6 but is now improving. Your kidneys are recovering after the catheter was replaced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching your calcium and phosphate—they’re low. We’ve started vitamin D and will give supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood cell count is coming down—from 25.8 to 18. That means the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing is better. Lungs are clearer. We’ll keep the antibiotics going for a full 8-day course as recommended by infectious disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your feeding tube nutrition is running smoothly. We cleared a clog yesterday with a flush.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We spoke with your son. He confirmed you’re able to make decisions. You refused a PICC line for antibiotics at home, which is okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So instead, you’ll stay here to finish all 8 days of IV antibiotics. That means discharge will be delayed by a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was high at first—3.4—so we held your warfarin. Now it’s low, under 2, so we’ve started enoxaparin injections to prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing your warfarin dose to 5 mg daily. Once your INR is stable, you can stop the injections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a midline for IV access. It’s easier than a PICC and will last through your antibiotic course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The midline was placed successfully. You’re doing well with it—no pain or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your fentanyl patch is back on. We held it at first because of confusion, but now it’s safe to restart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also increased your oral morphine for pain from your pressure ulcers. You’ve been taking up to 15 mg a few times a day without issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Palliative care visited. They suggest keeping your current pain plan and considering methadone later. For now, we’ll stick with what’s working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your blood cultures came back negative. No bloodstream infection. Urine culture showed yeast, but we won’t treat it unless you have symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is excellent now—creatinine is 0.2. Your electrolytes are stabilizing with supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your Foley catheter kinked yesterday, causing discomfort. The nurses flushed it and it’s working fine. We couldn’t upsize it, so we’ll teach your nursing home team to flush it if flow drops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re nearing the end of your antibiotic course. One more day of IV cefepime, then you’ll be ready for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send instructions to your nursing home: continue warfarin at 5 mg, give enoxaparin twice daily until INR is stable, and start daily vitamin D.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, increase morphine to 15 mg every 4 hours as needed. And flush the Foley if output slows—use 100 cc saline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final day of IV antibiotics. You’ve completed the full 8-day course. Your lungs are clear, and labs are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll remove the midline today. You’re ready to go back to the nursing home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your son confirmed he doesn’t want hospice discussed, but palliative care will help with pain management at the facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re being discharged today to extended care. You’ve recovered well from pneumonia and kidney injury.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember: take warfarin daily, use enoxaparin until INR is checked, take vitamin D, and use morphine for pain. Flush the Foley if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your code status remains DNR/DNI, as discussed with your family. We’ll follow up with your care team to ensure smooth transition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Stay hydrated, and your nursing home will monitor for any signs of infection or breathing issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check your vitamin D levels soon and adjust if needed. Otherwise, keep up with your routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any questions? Just nod if you’re okay with everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright. The transport team will take you shortly. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll call your facility to confirm they received all instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You responded well to treatment. The main concerns were pneumonia, high potassium, and kidney injury—all resolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is better controlled now with increased morphine. We’ll keep monitoring through your care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just rest now. You’re on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re proud of your progress. See you soon for follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll make sure your team knows everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set for discharge. Rest well.
